analysis.title: "Until The AI CapEx Debt Creation Machine Turns Back On": Goldman Says Credit Is Calm... For About Two More Months
key_insights: Goldman's IG credit desk (Jeffrey Papai) is a buyer of the current dip for the short/medium term. Seasonals turn positive in Q4, and he sees a clear runway in credit until AI capex debt issuance resumes in a couple of months.

IG credit, especially non-TMT, has held up through a bond selloff, a rate vol spike, the start of a Fed hiking cycle and French contagion. In the six weeks after Jackson Hole, IG funds took in a net $12B (65th percentile since 2020), including $5B last week versus a roughly $3B weekly average this year.

Index spreads are only 1bp wider from Aug 15 to Oct 15. In prior hiking cycles, spreads widened 27bps in 2015/16 and 15bps in 2022 from a month before to a month after the first hike. Even with MOVE above 110, spreads stayed within 10bps of their local tights.
Index yield hit 6% for only the third time since the financial crisis while spreads barely moved.

Buy-the-dip history: since 2024, buying when the index is at least 7bps off its 60-day tights has been followed by spread tightening of roughly 2bps, 8bps and 12bps over 4, 8 and 12 weeks (approximate, read off the chart). When MOVE starts a month above 100 and falls at least 10%, IG spreads have rallied about 10bps on average, versus a 3bp widening when vol stays elevated.

Investors are requiring less additional compensation than ever to hold corporates over sovereigns. About 25% of French corporate bonds trade inside OATs, and the IG index spread fell below 13% of total yield for the first time last month (record low). That share was above 80% at the 2008 and 2020 peaks.

The AI borrowers trade worse than the rest of the index. Excluding ORCL, MSFT, GOOGL, AMZN, META, NVDA, AMD, SPCX and AVGO, the ex-AI index trades roughly 2-2.5bps tighter than the full index, versus about 0.5bp wider a year ago (approximate, read off the chart). Those nine names grew from under 4% to over 6% of index market value and from under 5% to nearly 8% of duration.
Broadcom's 5Y CDS printed a record 136bp last week and Oracle's a record 261bp. Broadcom has lined up roughly $145B of chip debt for its customers (per ZeroHedge).

The calm reflects a gap in AI supply. There have been 23 AI deals of $3B or more since September 2025, worth $378B, with none in September or October. Papai says that if no deal comes in the balance of October, it will be the first two-month stretch since the capex build started without a $3B+ AI deal.

Goldman's AI credit basket blew out at the start of issuance waves (+16.7bps Oct 2025, +18.1bps Feb, +11.8bps June, +20.5bps July) and rallied in quiet months (May, September). Recent weeks are the second-best period for AI credit in the past year, behind May's supply holiday.

Net supply is expected to be roughly zero in Q4. Quarters with under $100B of net supply have averaged a 2.5bp rally since 2014, versus a 1bp selloff in heavier quarters. Combined with Q4 seasonals, this underpins the 'Santa Claus spread rally' view.

About $150B of announced chip financing is lined up: AVGO/Anthropic TPUs $60B (APCHIP 2.0), AVGO/OpenAI $30-50B ('Jalapeno'), SPCX/Nvidia GPUs $40B, AMZN/Nvidia GPUs $8.5B, ORCL/Nvidia GPUs no amount given. Another $20B+ of APCHIP 1.0 is still waiting to fund.

Because GPUs and TPUs depreciate fast, chip debt will be short-dated (under 7 years). Papai estimates $275B of 7-year-and-under AI issuance in 2027, or 20-25% of front-end IG supply, versus about 10% this year, 4% in 2025 and about 1% in 2024. He expects higher new-issue concessions for non-AI front-end paper and credit curves to flatten over 2027.

Insurers are the main buyers of AI front-end paper, citing attractive yields versus generic IG and confidence in frontier tech credit quality, partly based on the borrowers' market caps. Chip deals pay about 140bps over Goldman's 5-year IG basket (roughly 3x the spread) versus hyperscaler 30-years at 60bps over non-AI 30-years (about 1.5x). ZeroHedge's own napkin math puts chip paper near 220bps against a 79bp generic 5-year.

JPMorgan and Goldman declined to underwrite a $3.7B GPU loan for AI startup Volta Infrastructure, which drew more than $5B of orders, mainly from private credit, hedge funds and mutual funds (per ZeroHedge/Bloomberg).

Papai's trade: long GSIB 10-year bank paper (GSUCIBNK) into bank earnings. The bank basket spread versus the GS100 has peaked at bank earnings in each of the past five quarters, with a material relative rally afterwards in three of the four prior cases. He cites high expected bank supply (Citi and Wells issued off-cycle in September) and would also keep buying dips in non-AI 30-years (GSIG30NH).

ZeroHedge's editorial view is that the note is bearish in reverse: record-low compensation for corporate risk, AI borrowers trading wider while growing in the index, and calm that depends on their absence. It argues dip-buyers should sell into the Q4 rally, not after it.

tension_points.bull_case: Zero net supply, positive Q4 seasonals, receding rate vol and a two-month AI supply holiday set up a Q4 spread rally. History supports buying dips, with spreads tightening roughly 2bps, 8bps and 12bps over 4, 8 and 12 weeks.
tension_points.bear_case: ZeroHedge argues the calm exists only because AI borrowers are absent. Corporate spreads are at a record-low share of yield, and $150B of chip debt and $275B of front-end AI paper in 2027 will return. It says dip-buyers should sell into the rally.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Return of AI supply: a $3B+ AI deal in October would break the two-month gap, and the Papai call lasts only until closer to 2027 AI supply.

tension_points.bull_case: Insurers see attractive yields and confidence in frontier tech credit quality, with market caps as a core argument for lending.
tension_points.bear_case: Chip debt pays about 3x the spread of the 5-year IG basket, and lending against market cap fails if equity values fall. JPMorgan and Goldman declined to underwrite the Volta loan.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A sharp fall in the borrowers' equity values, such as the 9.3% weekly drop in Goldman's memory basket, would undermine the market-cap collateral argument.

theme_stances.key_argument: Short-dated chip debt will hit the front end of the curve that every other corporate borrower uses, raising new-issue concessions for non-AI front-end paper.
Seasonals turn positive, net supply is about zero, rate vol is receding and AI issuance is paused, so the dip is a short/medium-term buy.
theme_stances.evidence: the current dip I think is one to buy for the short/medium term
